summary: Multiplexed fallback pressure from single tenant causing thin-provisioning and transient throughput compression
description: Issue summary: Nimbus Health reports intermittent p99 and sustained p50 throughput loss on their dedicated pool during mid-day windows. Impact: requests are being routed to lower-tier fallback variants and autoscaler is shrinking the pool; customer sees ~30-40% reduction in sustained throughput for batched routes and elevated error retry rates. Environment: dedicated pool (dedicated-nyc-a) serving Nimbus Health, prod - us-east. Observed pattern suggests a single tenant producing many short, high-fanout multiplexed streams which trigger rapid fallback routing and thin-provisioning decisions by the autoscaler.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Customer generates many short chatlet streams (avg length 8 tokens, 150ms pacing) multiplexed across 2k concurrent sessions
2) Observe autoscaler downscaling decisions in dedicated-nyc-a around the same time window
3) Check routing logs: a subset of Nimbus sessions hit rate limit and are routed to fallback smaller-quantized variants
4) Measure throughput (tokens/sec) and p99 latency on affected batched route for 15 minute windows before/during/after the surge

investigation_notes: Initial hypothesis: noisy-tenant burst of short multiplexer streams is causing rapid slot fragmentation and autoscaler misclassification leading to premature scale-downs.
Telemetry: kernel-level nvlink and IPC did not show device-level thermal events; GPU utilization across pool was uneven (many GPUs at 5-10% p50, some at 95% p90).
KV-cache growth: observed transient spike in kv-cache entries for the noisy tenant which increased attachment time for subsequent batches (see kv-cache log snippet above).
Scheduler behavior: allocator logs show frequent small-lease grabs from the same tenant which starved larger batchers (allocator lease churn).
Routing: fallback policy kicked in when slot attach latency exceeded 250ms, which increased per-token cost and reduced batching efficiency for the customer.
Cross-check: no infra jobs or snapshotter activity coincident with the drop; related issue SUP-331122 captured a similar allocation pattern but different tenant.
Temporary mitigation tested: applied per-tenant short-stream throttling (soft limit) and increased dedicated-nyc-a min_pool_size from 6 -> 9 which stabilized throughput in a 30 minute trial.
Further action: propose autoscaler tuning to use fanout-aware heuristics and add tenant-level small-stream detection for preemptive soft-throttles.
